classification.difficultyReason: Explains why linear factors differing by a nonzero constant represent the same rational zero.

content.prompt:
Bob found that for a particular polynomial $P(x)$ that $P\left(\frac12\right)=0$. However, upon checking the suggested solutions, $\left(x-\frac12\right)$ was not given as a factor.

Explain why it is still considered a valid factor.

answer.short:
$x-\frac12$ is a valid factor; $2x-1=2\left(x-\frac12\right)$.

A nonzero constant multiplier can be absorbed into the other factor.
answer.worked:
By the factor theorem, $P\left(\frac12\right)=0$ means $x-\frac12$ is a factor.

The solutions may list $2x-1$, since
$$2x-1=2\left(x-\frac12\right).$$
If $P(x)=(2x-1)Q(x)$, then
$$P(x)=\left(x-\frac12\right)\bigl(2Q(x)\bigr).$$
Thus both forms are valid factors.
